latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Persistent or delayed antigenic stimulation from recent SARS-CoV-2 infection (typically 2–6 weeks prior), proposed to drive aberrant adaptive immunity (possible spike S1 superantigen-like activity, autoantibodies, immune complex formation) that initiates post-acute hyperinflammation in MIS-A.

Dysregulated hyperinflammatory cascade emerging 2–6 weeks after acute SARS-CoV-2 infection, integrating innate (macrophage, neutrophil) and adaptive (autoantibody, T-cell) responses to produce multi-organ injury distinct from acute viral pneumonia.
IL-6 driven hepatic acute-phase response, dominant cytokine pathway elevating CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin, and ESR while suppressing albumin in MIS-A.
NLRP3/inflammasome activation contributing to fever, endothelial activation, and macrophage activation overlap; rationale for anakinra rescue.
Th1/IFN-γ pathway activation driving CXCL9/CXCL10 elevation, macrophage priming, and tissue infiltration; partially overlaps with secondary HLH/MAS-like features.
Systemic macrophage activation with hyperferritinemia and hypertriglyceridemia; in severe MIS-A may overlap with secondary HLH/MAS phenotype.
Immune-complex and endothelial-driven complement activation contributing to vasculopathy and microthrombosis in MIS-A.

Post-infectious autoantibody production (anti-endothelial, anti-cardiolipin, anti-cytokine antibodies described in MIS-A/MIS-C series) with immune-complex deposition contributing to multi-organ inflammation.
Diffuse endothelial activation and procoagulant state driving D-dimer elevation, microthrombosis, and clinical thrombotic events; central feature distinguishing MIS-A from sepsis.

Inflammatory injury of myocardium, conduction system, coronary endothelium, and pericardium producing troponin elevation, ventricular dysfunction (often with preserved or mildly reduced EF, cardiogenic shock in severe cases), arrhythmia, pericardial effusion, and rare coronary artery dilation.
Microvascular thrombosis-driven organ ischemia (renal, cardiac, cerebral, splanchnic) contributing to AKI, troponin elevation, and stroke risk.
Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, oral mucositis (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue), peripheral edema/erythema; Kawasaki-like overlap especially in younger adults.

Mesenteric/intestinal inflammation producing severe abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, mesenteric lymphadenopathy, occasional pseudo-appendicitis or terminal ileitis on imaging; hypovolemia from GI losses contributes to shock.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: MIS-A mixed distributive / cardiogenic shock physiology
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Combined vasoplegic (cytokine-driven vasodilation) and cardiogenic (myocardial dysfunction) shock physiology with capillary leak; differs from sepsis by frequent cardiac dysfunction and absence of dominant respiratory source.

MIS-A clinically mimics bacterial septic shock (fever, hypotension, elevated CRP/procalcitonin, organ dysfunction) so empiric antimicrobials are routinely started; this axis tracks the diagnostic ambiguity that drives empiric coverage early.

Cumulative immunosuppression burden from corticosteroids, IVIG-related fluid/AKI risk, and IL-1/IL-6 blockade (anakinra/tocilizumab) increasing nosocomial and opportunistic infection risk during MIS-A treatment.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: MIS-A characteristically emerges 2–6 weeks after recognized or unrecognized SARS-CoV-2 infection; antigenic persistence and aberrant adaptive responses initiate the delayed hyperinflammatory cascade.
Post-infectious B-cell maturation produces autoantibodies (anti-endothelial, anti-cytokine, antiphospholipid) and immune complexes contributing to multi-organ inflammation.
Hyperinflammatory cascade strongly upregulates IL-6 secretion driving acute-phase reactant pattern.
Inflammasome activation co-drives systemic inflammation and is the pharmacologic target of anakinra in MIS-A/MIS-C.
Th1/IFN-γ activation drives CXCL9 elevation and macrophage priming; overlap with HLH/MAS phenotype.
Cytokine cascade activates the reticuloendothelial macrophage compartment producing hyperferritinemia.
Cytokines and immune complexes activate endothelium triggering procoagulant phenotype and microvascular injury.
Immune complexes activate classical complement pathway producing detectable C3/C4 consumption.
Anti-endothelial and antiphospholipid antibodies amplify endothelial activation and prothrombotic state.
Procoagulant endothelium produces microvascular thrombosis driving organ ischemia.
Cytokine-mediated and possibly autoantibody-mediated myocardial inflammation is the most clinically prominent organ involvement in MIS-A.
Coronary microvascular dysfunction and microthrombosis amplify myocardial injury beyond direct inflammation.
Kawasaki-like mucocutaneous features (conjunctivitis, rash, mucositis) reflect systemic vasculitis-like inflammation.
Mesenteric/intestinal inflammation produces severe abdominal pain frequently mistaken for surgical abdomen.
Acute ventricular dysfunction contributes a cardiogenic component to MIS-A shock.
Cytokine-mediated vasoplegia and capillary leak produce a distributive shock component.
GI fluid losses (vomiting/diarrhea) and third-spacing add hypovolemic component to shock physiology.
IL-6 drives hepatic CRP synthesis; CRP is markedly elevated (often >100 mg/L) in MIS-A.
IL-6-driven fibrinogen elevation prolongs ESR.
Acute-phase fibrinogen synthesis is upregulated; falling fibrinogen suggests overlap with consumptive coagulopathy or MAS.
Negative acute-phase reactant suppression plus capillary leak lowers albumin.
Direct measurement of the driving cytokine when assayed.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Often modestly elevated even without bacterial infection, contributing to the sepsis-mimic problem.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: PCT is non-specifically elevated by intense systemic inflammation, complicating discrimination from bacterial sepsis.
IL-1β is a major endogenous pyrogen producing the persistent fever (≥38°C ≥24 h) required by the CDC case definition.
Macrophage activation drives marked hyperferritinemia; very high values (>10 000 ng/mL) suggest MAS-like overlap.
Macrophage-driven lipoprotein lipase suppression elevates triglycerides; component of HLH-2004 criteria when MIS-A overlaps MAS/HLH.
Reflects T-cell/macrophage activation; HLH/MAS-like elevation in severe MIS-A.
CXCL9 is a sensitive readout of IFN-γ axis activity.
Microthrombosis and fibrin turnover markedly elevate D-dimer; near-universal in MIS-A.
Endothelial activation, consumption, and macrophage activation drive thrombocytopenia (more frequent than in acute COVID-19).
Lymphopenia is a frequent laboratory feature in MIS-A driven by cytokine-mediated lymphocyte redistribution and apoptosis.
Neutrophilia accompanies acute hyperinflammation; combined neutrophilia + lymphopenia is typical.
Myocardial inflammation produces troponin elevation in a majority of hospitalized MIS-A cases.
Direct hazard pathway for clinically diagnosed myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction.
Drives acute myocardial injury events including arrhythmia and ventricular dysfunction.
Polymorphous (often morbilliform or maculopapular) rash; one of CDC mucocutaneous criteria.
Red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, oral mucositis as Kawasaki-like features.
Severe abdominal pain is one of the most prominent presenting symptoms, sometimes mimicking appendicitis.
Mixed shock physiology lowers MAP requiring vasopressor support.
Hypotension with SBP <90 mmHg meets CDC shock criterion for MIS-A.
Compensatory tachycardia for fever and hypovolemia/vasoplegia; conduction abnormalities may also alter rhythm.
Hypoperfusion and microvascular dysfunction elevate lactate.
Renal microvascular injury plus shock-related ATN raises creatinine.
AKI is a frequent complication driven by combined ischemic, inflammatory, and microthrombotic injury.
MIS-A patients have markedly increased risk of venous and arterial thrombosis (PE, DVT, stroke, MI) requiring anticoagulation strategy.
Cerebral microvascular thrombosis and macrothrombosis raise stroke risk.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Hypoxemia in MIS-A is most often cardiogenic (pulmonary edema) rather than primary alveolar; severe ARDS suggests alternative or co-existing acute COVID-19.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Capillary leak, pulmonary edema, and rare diffuse alveolar injury contribute to respiratory failure risk.
Severe MIS-A overlaps MAS/secondary HLH (very high ferritin, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia, hepatosplenomegaly).
Hepatic involvement (transaminitis) is common from inflammation, congestion, and shock liver components.
Same inflammatory/ischemic hepatic injury raises AST.
Tissue injury and inflammation increase LDH.
Immune-complex mediated complement consumption lowers C3.
Classical pathway activation reduces C4.
Renal hypoperfusion drops urine output; an early bedside marker of shock severity.
Multi-organ dysfunction raises composite SOFA score.
Refractory shock is the dominant proximal cause of death in MIS-A.
Severe ventricular dysfunction and arrhythmia drive cardiac mortality risk.
Pulmonary embolism, stroke, and cardiac thrombosis contribute to mortality.
MAS/HLH overlap markedly worsens prognosis.
Treatment-related immunosuppression and ICU exposure raise nosocomial infection mortality.
Cumulative steroid + IVIG + biologic exposure plus invasive devices raise nosocomial infection risk.
Indistinguishability from septic shock at presentation drives universal empiric antibiotic exposure even when ultimately MIS-A.
The disease can present with persistent or recurrent fever over the observed clinical history.
MIS-A can mimic sepsis but is driven by delayed post-infectious hyperinflammation.
Pulmonary, cardiac, serosal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement can cause dyspnea.
Pulmonary or airway involvement can cause cough.

axes.shape_free_text: Persistent fever ≥38°C lasting ≥24 h is a CDC defining feature; often spiking to 39–40°C, persists despite empiric antibiotics, and rapidly defervesces with IVIG/steroids.
Sinus tachycardia from fever and shock; conduction abnormalities (AV block, bundle branch block) reported in subset.
Frequently low at admission (<90 mmHg meets shock criterion); responds variably to fluids alone, often requires vasopressors.
Often <65 mmHg requiring vasopressors; recovers within several days with immunomodulation.
Tachypnea common from fever, shock, and pulmonary edema; severe hypoxemic respiratory failure favors alternative diagnosis.
Usually normal or mildly reduced unless cardiogenic pulmonary edema; severe hypoxemia (<90% on supplemental O2) suggests acute COVID-19 ARDS rather than MIS-A predominance.
Oliguria during shock phase; recovers with hemodynamic stabilization unless ATN established.
Frequently elevated with neutrophilia + lymphopenia; modest leukocytosis 10–20 ×10^9/L typical.
Neutrophilia 8–18 ×10^9/L typical; left-shift common.
Lymphopenia (<1.0) is a near-universal feature; recovers with treatment.
Thrombocytopenia frequent (often 80–150); profound thrombocytopenia raises concern for DIC or MAS overlap.
Mild anemia common from inflammation; falling hemoglobin with elevated LDH and schistocytes raises MAHA/TMA concern.
Hallmark marked elevation, typically >100 mg/L and often >200 mg/L; falls within days of effective immunomodulation.
Markedly elevated; supports systemic inflammation per CDC criteria.
Marked hyperferritinemia (often 1 000–10 000 ng/mL); values >10 000 should prompt MAS/HLH evaluation.
Often modestly elevated even without bacterial infection; not a reliable discriminator from sepsis in MIS-A.
Markedly elevated when measured; correlates with disease severity.
Elevated; reflects IFN-γ axis activity and overlaps with HLH/MAS biomarker pattern.
Elevated when MAS/HLH overlap present.
Initially elevated as acute-phase reactant (300–800); paradoxical fall <250 with rising D-dimer/ferritin suggests MAS/HLH or DIC overlap and worsens prognosis.
axes.second_peak: May fall sharply (<150 mg/dL) in severe MAS/HLH overlap or DIC

axes.shape_free_text: Markedly elevated, often >5 µg/mL FEU; central feature linking MIS-A to its prothrombotic phenotype.
Mild prolongation common; significant prolongation suggests DIC, hepatic dysfunction, or MAS overlap.
Mildly prolonged; antiphospholipid antibody-related lupus anticoagulant effect occasionally reported.
Elevated in majority of hospitalized MIS-A; magnitude correlates with myocardial injury/myocarditis severity.
AKI common during shock phase; usually recovers but may require RRT in severe cases.
Rises in parallel with creatinine during AKI/shock.
Elevated during shock phase; persistent elevation predicts worse outcome.
Decreased with metabolic acidosis from shock and AKI.
Hyponatremia (130–134) common from SIADH-like, GI losses, and capillary leak.
Decreased from negative acute-phase response and capillary leak; correlates with severity.
Mild-to-moderate transaminitis common (often 50–300 U/L); marked elevation suggests shock liver or MAS.
Often elevated in parallel with ALT; AST > ALT pattern suggests ischemic hepatitis or MAS.
Elevated from tissue injury and hemolysis when present.
Elevated in MAS/HLH overlap; typically 250–1000 mg/dL when present.
Often low-normal or modestly decreased reflecting consumption.
May be low reflecting classical pathway activation.
Transient antiphospholipid positivity reported in subset; may not persist.
Often 4–12 at admission with shock; high SOFA correlates with mortality.
Polymorphous rash (morbilliform, maculopapular, occasionally urticarial); may include palmoplantar erythema/desquamation.
Red cracked lips, strawberry tongue, oropharyngeal hyperemia; bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis often coexists.
Severe diffuse or RLQ pain, sometimes mistaken for appendicitis; vomiting and diarrhea common.
Frequent presenting symptom; may accompany altered mental status.
Encephalopathy from inflammation, hypoperfusion, or cerebrovascular events.
Common prodromal feature alongside fever.
Cervical lymphadenopathy may be present (Kawasaki-like criterion).
Pleuritic or substernal pain from myopericarditis.
Imaging often shows pulmonary edema or small effusions rather than dense alveolar infiltrates; bilateral GGO with severe hypoxemia favors acute COVID-19 pneumonia rather than MIS-A predominance.

MIS-A typically lacks valvular vegetations; reused as generic echocardiographic ventricular dysfunction proxy in absence of dedicated axis is inappropriate — keep low; mild functional MR may occur with LV dysfunction.
Substantially increased during peak inflammatory phase; clinically diagnosed myocarditis in a large minority of cases.
Driven by direct inflammation and microvascular ischemia; manifests as troponin elevation, arrhythmia, ventricular dysfunction.
Increased venous and arterial thrombosis risk (PE, DVT, stroke, MI) compared to non-MIS-A inpatients with similar severity.
Elevated relative to age-matched controls due to thrombotic and embolic mechanisms.
Common during shock phase; KDIGO stage 2–3 in severe cases.
Lower than acute COVID-19 ARDS but possible from cardiogenic edema or overlapping infection.
Subset of MIS-A meets HLH-2004 / MS-2009 criteria; very high ferritin, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia.
Nosocomial infection risk during prolonged ICU stay and immunosuppressive treatment.
Increased during therapeutic anticoagulation, particularly with thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy.
Used here as proxy for refractory shock progression in MIS-A.
Tracks how strongly the presentation resembles bacterial sepsis at the moment of decision-making.
True concomitant bacterial infection cannot be excluded early; persistently positive cultures or clear bacterial source raises this axis and shifts management away from pure immunomodulation.
Cumulative iatrogenic immunosuppression burden during MIS-A treatment.
Modulates anticoagulation intensity decisions.
Confidence MIS-A is overlapping with secondary HLH/MAS, raising threshold to add anakinra/etoposide-style escalation.
Pre-test probability of recent SARS-CoV-2 exposure/infection (within 12 weeks); a CDC requirement for diagnosis.
Modulates safety of QT-prolonging supportive medications during ICU course.

Aggregate mortality hazard reflecting shock, myocardial injury, thrombosis, MAS, and secondary infection contributions; declines rapidly after effective immunomodulation. Reported case-fatality 5–15% in published series.
History-level fever burden over days to months, distinct from a single measured body temperature.

axes.display_name: Lack of clinical response to standard antibacterial therapy
axes.shape_free_text: Persistent fever, inflammation, or organ findings despite antibacterial therapy that should have covered ordinary bacterial infection.
Patient-reported or observed breathlessness from pulmonary, cardiac, mediastinal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement.
Dry or productive cough as a symptom axis; mechanism depends on pulmonary, airway, cardiac, or mediastinal involvement.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Especially when ferritin >10 000 ng/mL — suggests MAS/HLH overlap with consumptive coagulopathy.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Rising ferritin with falling fibrinogen is a classical MAS/HLH signature requiring escalation (anakinra, consideration of HLH-directed therapy).
Troponin rise precedes or accompanies clinically diagnosed myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction.
Markedly elevated D-dimer (>3–5 µg/mL FEU) clinically motivates therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation in MIS-A.
Thrombocytopenia worsens bleeding risk under anticoagulation, complicating thrombosis management.
Persistent lactate elevation in shock reflects refractory hypoperfusion and predicts mortality.
CRP serves as bedside readout of overall hyperinflammatory drive; trajectory tracks response to immunomodulation.
Sepsis-mimic features drive higher empiric antimicrobial intensity until cultures clarify etiology.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cardiac and Kawasaki-like phenotype is the strongest indication; benefit is most pronounced in this subgroup.
Large fluid load (1–2 g/kg over 8–24 h) can worsen pulmonary edema in cardiogenic shock; titrate over longer infusion or split dosing.
IVIG-associated AKI risk increases in pre-existing renal disease and with sucrose-stabilized formulations.

failure_modes: Insufficient response in pure cytokine-storm phenotype without Kawasaki-like features
Rebound after single dose when steroids not co-administered
Volume overload in severe LV dysfunction

side_effects.interpretation: Thrombotic complications, especially with rapid infusion

treatments.context_specific_role: Foundational immunomodulation for MIS-A, particularly when Kawasaki-like or myocardial features dominate; combined with corticosteroids in current treatment paradigm.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Broad cytokine suppression; pulse 1–2 mg/kg/day or methylprednisolone pulses 10–30 mg/kg/day in severe disease.
Untreated bacterial sepsis must be ruled out / covered before immunosuppression; otherwise steroid worsens infection.
Pulse-dose steroids accelerate hemodynamic recovery in shock-predominant MIS-A.

failure_modes: Hyperglycemia and steroid psychosis complicating ICU course

side_effects.interpretation: Suppression of innate/adaptive immunity raises secondary infection risk
Mineralocorticoid effect / restoration of vascular tone

treatments.context_specific_role: Co-foundational with IVIG; pulse-dose preferred for severe shock or MAS-overlap presentations; tapered over 2–4 weeks.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Most effective when MAS/HLH-overlap features (very high ferritin, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia) are present.
Direct IL-1 pathway target — strongest effect when IL-1 axis dominates.
Active uncontrolled bacterial/fungal infection is a relative contraindication; short half-life allows rapid discontinuation if infection emerges.

failure_modes: Insufficient response when IFN-γ axis dominates
treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue therapy for steroid-refractory MIS-A or MAS/HLH overlap; preferred over tocilizumab when concomitant infection cannot be excluded due to short half-life.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Direct IL-6 receptor blockade with strongest effect in IL-6-dominant phenotype.
Long half-life (2–3 weeks) and infection masking risk make tocilizumab inappropriate in active uncontrolled infection.
Hepatotoxicity risk increases with baseline transaminase elevation.

failure_modes: Masking of secondary bacterial infection due to CRP suppression
GI perforation in patients with severe mucosal inflammation

side_effects.interpretation: Increased infection risk with infection masking

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative biologic rescue when IL-6 axis dominates and infection adequately ruled out; less preferred when infection uncertainty is high.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Kawasaki-like phenotype with concern for coronary artery involvement justifies antiplatelet prophylaxis.
Platelet count <80 ×10^9/L raises bleeding risk above benefit.

treatments.context_specific_role: Anti-platelet prophylaxis especially when Kawasaki-like / coronary involvement suspected; held if profound thrombocytopenia.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: High prothrombotic burden justifies therapeutic-intensity anticoagulation in many series.
Markedly elevated D-dimer (>3–5 µg/mL FEU) commonly triggers therapeutic dosing.
Active bleeding or severe thrombocytopenia restricts to prophylactic dose or holding.
Renal clearance — switch to UFH or anti-Xa monitoring at CrCl <30 mL/min.

treatments.context_specific_role: Routine VTE prophylaxis at minimum, escalated to therapeutic dosing for confirmed thrombosis or very high D-dimer with cardiac/multiorgan involvement.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: First-line vasopressor in MIS-A shock; supports MAP while immunomodulation takes effect.

failure_modes: Refractory shock requiring additional vasopressors / inotropes
Peripheral / digital ischemia at very high doses
treatments.context_specific_role: Hemodynamic bridge during shock phase pending immunomodulatory response.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Inodilator support for cardiogenic shock with reduced LVEF in MIS-A myocarditis.
Vasodilatory effect can worsen hypotension — pair with vasopressor.

treatments.context_specific_role: Inotropic support for severe LV dysfunction in MIS-A myocarditis.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: MIS-A is clinically indistinguishable from septic shock at presentation; empiric coverage standard until cultures clarify.
Negative cultures at 48–72 h with classic MIS-A features support de-escalation.

failure_modes: Unnecessary prolonged exposure if MIS-A diagnosis confirmed and cultures negative
treatments.context_specific_role: Universal empiric cover at presentation; de-escalated within 48–72 h once bacterial sepsis adequately ruled out and MIS-A diagnosis established.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Indicated only if concomitant active acute COVID-19 pneumonia with hypoxemia coexists; pure MIS-A does not require antiviral.

failure_modes: Inappropriate use when no active acute COVID-19 pneumonia component
treatments.context_specific_role: Used only when MIS-A overlaps with active acute COVID-19 pneumonia; not part of standard MIS-A regimen otherwise.

present_within_2_to_6_weeks.trajectory_modulation: Defines the disease — required for diagnosis per CDC criteria.

absent_or_remote_>12_weeks.trajectory_modulation: MIS-A diagnosis is excluded without temporally linked SARS-CoV-2 evidence.

age_20_to_50.trajectory_modulation: Most published cases cluster in 20s–40s; older adults are diagnosed less commonly but mortality may be higher.

age_>65.trajectory_modulation: Higher case-fatality when it does occur due to comorbidity burden.

male.trajectory_modulation: Modest male predominance reported in case series.

black_or_hispanic.trajectory_modulation: Disproportionate representation in U.S. case series, partially reflecting epidemiologic exposure and access patterns rather than biologic susceptibility.

unvaccinated.trajectory_modulation: Vaccination is associated with markedly lower MIS-A incidence.

bmi_>30.trajectory_modulation: Higher severity and worse outcomes with obesity; often with diabetes/hypertension co-occurrence.

present.trajectory_modulation: Worsens shock physiology, AKI risk, and infection susceptibility during steroid therapy.
Higher risk of severe cardiac dysfunction and mortality.

supportive_care: Early ICU admission with continuous cardiac telemetry given high arrhythmia and myocarditis risk
Echocardiography on admission and serial monitoring of LV function; cardiac MRI when feasible to characterize myocardial involvement
Daily inflammatory marker trend (CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, D-dimer, troponin) to monitor treatment response and detect MAS/HLH transition
Cautious fluid resuscitation balanced against cardiogenic component of shock; norepinephrine first-line vasopressor
Inotropic support (milrinone, dobutamine) with mechanical circulatory support escalation (IABP, VA-ECMO) for refractory cardiogenic shock
VTE prophylaxis universally; therapeutic anticoagulation for confirmed thrombosis, severe ventricular dysfunction, or markedly elevated D-dimer per institutional protocol
Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics on admission with rapid de-escalation as cultures and SARS-CoV-2 serology/PCR clarify diagnosis
Targeted glycemic control during corticosteroid therapy
Stress ulcer and DVT prophylaxis per ICU protocols
Renal protection: avoid nephrotoxins, dose-adjust antimicrobials, anticipate need for renal replacement therapy
Daily neurologic assessment for stroke and encephalopathy; low threshold for neuroimaging given thrombotic risk
Multidisciplinary team: cardiology, infectious disease, rheumatology/immunology, intensivist, hematology
Post-discharge cardiac follow-up at 2–6 weeks with repeat echocardiography; cardiac MRI for persistent dysfunction
Counsel on completing SARS-CoV-2 vaccination after recovery (typically delayed ~90 days); recurrence risk discussion
Screen for and treat antiphospholipid antibodies if thrombosis occurred and consider extended anticoagulation duration based on persistence at repeat testing
